properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 2:00PM PDT by NWS San Diego CA
properties.description:
HLSSGX

This product covers EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA

**Impacts from Tropical Storm Rachel Expected in San Diego County
Late Tonight through Early Sunday Afternoon**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for San Diego County
Coastal Areas, San Diego County Deserts, San Diego County
Mountains, and San Diego County Valleys

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 440 miles south of San Mateo Point CA or about 390 miles
south of Mouth of Tijuana River CA
- 27.0N 118.3W
- Storm Intensity 65 mph
- Movement North-northeast or 25 degrees at 30 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Storm Rachel is currently about 400 miles south of San Diego,
moving north-northeast towards Northern Baja at about 30 mph. Rachel
is expected to make landfall south of the US/Mexico Border tonight.
Tropical storm level impacts will likely affect San Diego County. A
Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for all of San Diego County. The main
concerns with Tropical Storm Rachel are coastal flooding, wind, and
periods of heavy rain which could lead to localized flooding and flash
flooding. The majority of impacts from the tropical storm are expected
late tonight through early Sunday afternoon.

South swell from Tropical Storm Rachel will arrive on Sunday. The
combination of south and northwest swells, increased onshore winds,
and high tides over 7 feet will maintain a threat of coastal flooding
and beach erosion along area beaches. Surf on Sunday is currently
expected to peak at 6 to 9 feet, decreasing to 3 to 6 feet for Monday
and Tuesday. Confidence in impactful coastal flooding is high, with
significant coastal flooding and beach erosion likely.

Widespread rain is expected on Sunday from Tropical Storm Rachel.
There is expected to be a gradient in rainfall amounts with the higher
amounts on the southeastern side of the storm. Confidence is high that
the heaviest rain will occur over San Diego County mountains and
deserts. Peak rainfall rates of 0.50 to 0.60 inches are possible for
the coast and valleys, 0.50 to 0.70 inches per hour possible for the
deserts, and 0.70 to 1 inch per hour for the mountains. Current
forecast has rainfall totals of 0.50 to 1.25 inches for the coast,
valleys, and deserts and 1 to 2.5 inches for the mountains. Areas of
flash and urban flooding are probable, especially where the maximum
rainfall rates occur. The San Diego River at Fashion Valley is
currently forecast to peak at 8.0 feet (action/monitor stage) just
before noon on Sunday. Those with interests near the San Diego River
should continue to monitor the forecast.

Increased winds are expected with the onset and passage of Tropical
Storm Rachel. Sustained winds of 39+ mph are expected on the southeast
side of the storm. Based on the current track, more southern and
eastern parts of San Diego County are most likely to see winds of this
magnitude. Regardless, strong sustained winds and wind gusts can be
expected on Sunday. Winds will likely be enhanced by local terrain
with gusts 40 to 55 mph on the desert slopes of the mountains and into
the deserts. Local gusts up to 60 mph possible on mountain ridges and
in passes and canyons. Winds are expected to remain elevated in
Rachel's wake with continued strong gusts on the desert mountain
slopes into the deserts through Monday morning.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* OTHER COASTAL HAZARDS:
High tides over 7 ft, combined with high surf and gusty onshore winds
will increase the threat for coastal flooding across area beaches.
Additionally surf of 6 to 9 ft will create dangerous swimming
conditions. Significant coastal flooding and beach erosion is likely.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across San Diego County. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Prepare for dangerous rainfall flooding having possible significant
impacts across San Diego County.

* WIND:
Prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted, especially in coastal and valley locations that
don't typically experience strong winds. Some fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA, little to no impact
is anticipated.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the ocean, in a low-lying or poor drainage area, in a valley, or
near a river, plan to move to safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in San Diego CA around 8 PM PDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

* WHAT...DAMAGING sea-water coastal flooding is likely through
Sunday, especially near the Sunday morning high tide where
anticipated tide levels are expected to be around 8 feet. The
most likely areas for DAMAGING coastal flooding on Sunday
morning will be vulnerable south-facing beaches due to the
expected combination of very high level tide levels around 8
feet (including additive effect of low barometric pressure and
onshore winds gusting to 15 to 25 mph), high surf of 5 to 8
feet, and light to moderate rainfall. For all other beaches,
minor to moderate coastal flooding is expected near times of
high tide. From Sunday night through Tuesday, there will be the
continued threat of at least minor to moderate coastal flooding
and elevated surf across Los Angeles county beaches, especially
south facing shores. Dangerous rip currents are likely.

* WHERE...Malibu Coast and Los Angeles County Beaches.

* WHEN...For the Coastal Flood Warning, until 3 PM PDT Sunday.
For the High Surf Advisory, from 6 AM to 10 PM PDT Sunday. For
the Coastal Flood Advisory, from 3 PM Sunday to 2 PM PDT
Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...For vulnerable south-facing beaches (such as Alamitos
Peninsula and Naples in Long Beach as well as Malibu),
SIGNIFICANT sea- water flooding will likely DAMAGE coastal
structures and beach roadways around the time of high tide,
especially the Sunday morning high tide. In addition,
significant ponding of water on low-lying beach roadways could
make driving difficult. THERE IS GROWING CONFIDENCE THAT THE
EXPECTED COASTAL FLOODING IMPACTS ON SUNDAY MORNING FOR
VULNERABLE SOUTH FACING BEACHES OF LA COUNTY COULD BE THE MOST
SIGNIFICANT WE HAVE SEEN SO FAR THIS SEASON, INCLUDING THOSE
SEEN WITH MARIE. For all other beaches and harbors, shallow with
minor to moderate sea- water flooding will likely impact
beaches and walkways, especially with the Sunday morning high
tide which could cause local damage to most vulnerable locations
such as Venice. For all beach areas, significant erosion is
expected. There is an increased risk for ocean drowning.
Dangerous and life- threatening rip currents can pull swimmers
and surfers out to sea. Large breaking waves can cause injury,
wash people off beaches and rocks, and capsize small boats near
shore.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...High tides of around 8 feet are expected on
Sunday morning (nearly 2 feet above astronomical high tide of
6.1 feet), returning to around 7.5 feet for Monday and Tuesday
mornings. The projected high tides of around 8 feet for Sunday
morning would approach or exceed recent record tide levels for
LA county. Large secondary high tides are also expected each
evening.
properties.instruction:

Do NOT drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth.

Remain out of the water due to dangerous surf conditions, or stay
near occupied lifeguard towers. Rock jetties can be deadly in
such conditions, stay off the rocks.

creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- As Isaias weakens and moves northward into the lower Ohio Valley,
periods of rain will continue. While rainfall rates may decrease
in some areas this evening, short bursts of heavy rain are
possible through tonight. By Sunday morning, total accumulations
of generally 5 to 8 inches are expected along the
southeast-facing Blue Ridge Escarpment, with 2 to 5 inches
elsewhere in the watch area.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
A Flood Watch for flash flooding means there is a potential for rapid
onset flooding based on current forecasts. Flash flooding is a very
dangerous situation and may impact areas that do not typically flood.
Please monitor the latest forecasts and be prepared to take action
quickly should Flash Flood Warnings be issued.

Rainfall of more than five inches in similar storms has been
associated with an increased risk of landslides, especially
fast-moving debris flows and debris slides. If you live on a
mountainside or in a cove at the base of a mountain, especially near
a stream, be ready to leave in advance of the storm and follow
evacuation orders from local officials. Consider postponing travel
along mountain roads during the heavy rainfall event.

properties.description:
ESFPPG

An active trough to the north is projected to drift southward and
move over the territory by Tuesday of next week. This trough is
likely to remain strong and active through the duration of next
week, and may even intensify with embedded low pressure centers.
Widespread showers may be heavy and persistent at times with the
possibility of thunderstorms Tuesday through the weekend.
Widespread flash flooding may occur from this rainfall. Landslides
will be possible along steep mountainous terrain. While there is
still uncertainty in the exact magnitude and duration of rainfall,
plan now for wet conditions next Tuesday through at least Sunday.

Keep up to date with the latest forecast information through our
internet page (www.weather.gov/ppg), local media, social media,
and our NOAA Radio broadcasts.

properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 10 at 3:00PM EDT until October 12 at 2:00AM EDT by NWS Baltimore MD/Washington DC
properties.description:
Moderate to heavy rainfall is expected as the remnants of Isaias
track across the region starting early Sunday morning. Storms should
be highly efficient rainfall producers given the tropical nature of
the air mass. In particular, the eastern slopes of the Blue Ridge
have the potential to see the most rainfall given the continued
easterly upslope winds. A further eastward expansion of these watches
may be needed.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is possible.

* WHERE...Portions of central, northern, and northwest Virginia,
including the following areas, in central Virginia, Albemarle,
Central Virginia Blue Ridge, Greene, Nelson and Orange. In northern
Virginia, Culpeper, Northern Fauquier and Southern Fauquier. In
northwest Virginia, Madison, Northern Virginia Blue Ridge and
Rappahannock.

* WHEN...From late tonight through late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- The remnants of Isaias will bring a tropical air mass much into
the Mid-Atlantic region late tonight into Sunday. Storms should
be highly efficient in this environment and capable of producing
several inches of rain throughout the duration of the event.
Storm total rainfall is expected to be around 2 to 3 inches, with
pockets of 3 to 5 inches along the eastern slopes of the Blue
Ridge.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
You should monitor later forecasts and be alert for possible Flood
Warnings. Those living in areas prone to flooding should be prepared
to take action should flooding develop.

Visit https://www.aqmd.gov/alertinfo to check current and forecasted
air quality levels.

* WHERE...the Imperial Valley. Levels of particle pollution can vary
by time and location depending on emissions and local weather
conditions.

* WHEN...Sunday, October 11, 2026 from 12:00 AM until 10:00 PM.

* IMPACTS... Particle pollution can get deep into the lungs and
cause serious health problems such as asthma attacks, heart and lung
disease symptoms, and increased risk of lung infections. Everyone
can be affected, but sensitive groups such as people with lung or
heart disease, older adults, people who are pregnant, children, and
those who spend a lot of time outdoors are at greater risk.
properties.instruction:
To protect your health, check air quality levels and act as needed:

* When Air Quality Index (AQI) levels are "Unhealthy for
Sensitive Groups" (orange), sensitive groups as specified
above should limit extended or intense outdoor activity.
* When AQI is "Unhealthy" (red), everyone may experience health
impacts. Sensitive groups should avoid extended time outdoors.
* When AQI is "Very Unhealthy" (purple), sensitive groups should
avoid all outdoor physical activity. Everyone else should
avoid extended or intense outdoor activity.
* When AQI is "Hazardous" (maroon), everyone should avoid all
outdoor physical activity.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...

To help keep indoor air clean when air quality is poor:

* Keep windows and doors closed
* Run your air conditioner and/or an air purifier
* Do not use whole house fans or swamp coolers that bring in
outside air if you have other methods to stay cool
* Avoid other sources of pollution such as fireplaces, candles,
incense, grilling, and gasoline-powered lawn and garden
equipment

To help minimize outdoor particle pollution levels:

* Carpool, telecommute, reduce trips, or take public
transportation
* Slow down if driving on dirt roads
* Stabilize loose soils

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 10 at 8:07AM PDT by NWS San Diego CA
properties.description:
HLSSGX

This product covers EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA

**Impacts from Tropical Storm Rachel Expected in San Diego County Late
Tonight through Sunday Afternoon**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for San Diego County
Coastal Areas, San Diego County Deserts, San Diego County
Mountains, and San Diego County Valleys

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 560 miles south-southwest of San Mateo Point CA or about
510 miles south-southwest of Mouth of Tijuana River CA
- 25.5N 119.6W
- Storm Intensity 60 mph
- Movement Northeast or 55 degrees at 22 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Storm Rachel is currently about 520 miles south-southwest of
San Diego, moving northeast towards Northern Baja at about 22 mph.
Rachel is expected to make landfall somewhere just south of the
US/Mexico Border Saturday evening. Tropical storm level impacts will
likely affect San Diego County. A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for
all of San Diego County. The main concerns with Tropical Storm Rachel
are coastal flooding, wind, and periods of heavy rain which could lead
to localized flooding and flash flooding. The majority of impacts from
the tropical storm are expected late tonight through early Sunday
afternoon.

South swell from Tropical Storm Rachel will arrive on Sunday. The
combination of south and northwest swells, increased onshore winds,
and high tides over 7 feet will maintain a threat of coastal flooding
and beach erosion along area beaches. Surf on Sunday is currently
expected to peak at 6 to 9 feet, decreasing to 3 to 6 feet for Monday
and Tuesday. Confidence in impactful coastal flooding is high, with
significant coastal flooding and beach erosion likely.

Widespread rain is expected on Sunday from Tropical Storm Rachel.
There is expected to be a gradient in rainfall amounts with the higher
amounts on the southeastern side of the storm. Confidence is high that
the heaviest rain will occur over San Diego County mountains and
deserts. Peak rainfall rates of 0.50 to 0.60 inches are possible for
the coast and valleys, 0.50 to 0.70 inches per hour possible for the
deserts, and 0.70 to 1 inch per hour for the mountains. Current
forecast has rainfall totals of 0.50 to 1.25 inches for the coast,
valleys, and deserts and 1 to 2.5 inches for the mountains. Areas of
flash and urban flooding are probable, especially where the maximum
rainfall rates occur. The San Diego River at Fashion Valley is
currently forecast to peak at 7.4 feet (just below monitor stage)
Sunday afternoon. Those with interests near the San Diego River should
continue to monitor the forecast.

Increased winds are expected with the onset and passage of Tropical
Storm Rachel. Sustained winds of 39+ mph are expected on the southeast
side of the storm. Based on the current track, more southern and
eastern parts of San Diego County are most likely to see winds of this
magnitude. Regardless, strong sustained winds and wind gusts can be
expected on Sunday. Winds will likely be enhanced by local terrain
with gusts 40 to 55 mph on the desert slopes of the mountains and into
the deserts. Local gusts up to 60 mph possible on mountain ridges and
in passes and canyons. Winds are expected to remain elevated in
Rachel's wake with continued strong gusts on the desert mountain
slopes into the deserts through Monday morning.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* COASTAL HAZARDS:
High tides over 7 ft, combined with high surf and gusty onshore winds
will increase the threat for coastal flooding across area beaches.
Additionally surf of 6 to 9 ft will create dangerous swimming
conditions. Significant coastal flooding and beach erosion is likely.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across San Diego County. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Prepare for dangerous rainfall flooding having possible significant
impacts across San Diego County.

* WIND:
Prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted, especially in coastal and valley locations that
don't typically experience strong winds. Some fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA, little to no impact
is anticipated.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the ocean, in a low-lying or poor drainage area, in a valley, or
near a river, plan to move to safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in San Diego CA around 2 PM PDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.areaDesc: Lincoln; Lyon; Murray; Cottonwood; Pipestone; Kingsbury; Brookings; Lake; Moody
properties.headline: Special Weather Statement issued October 10 at 2:46AM CDT by NWS Sioux Falls SD
properties.description:
South winds gusting as high as 40 to 45 mph will develop quickly
by mid to late morning. Wind speeds will ease across east-central
South Dakota by mid afternoon, while the stronger gusts linger in
southwest Minnesota through sunset.

These strong winds, combined with near-record warmth and humidity
levels as low as 25 to 35 percent, will produce elevated fire
weather concerns today. Grassland fire danger will reach the High
category, with locally higher fire danger in cured croplands and
grasses.

Avoid outdoor burning and use extra caution with equipment in dry
crops, as rapid fire spread is possible.

In addition to the elevated fire danger, winds gusting over 40 mph
may produce areas of blowing dust, locally reducing visibility and
air quality.

NWSheadline: ELEVATED FIRE DANGER AND LOCALIZED BLOWING DUST TODAY

properties.areaDesc: Traverse; Big Stone; Marshall; Roberts; Day; Clark; Codington; Grant; Hamlin; Deuel
properties.headline: Special Weather Statement issued October 10 at 1:47AM CDT by NWS Aberdeen SD
properties.description:
Warm and dry conditions will combine with strong wind gusts today
to create elevated fire weather concerns over the area this
afternoon. Due to abnormal warmth, minimum afternoon humidity
will drop to 25 to 35 percent. Strong southerly winds are expected
this morning, gusting up to 25 to 35 miles per hour. Some
localized gusts up to 45 miles per hour will be possible. Winds
are expected to decrease through the afternoon, meaning that the
strongest winds will not coincide with the lowest afternoon
humidity. However, gusts up to 30 miles per hour may linger into
the afternoon. Grassland Fire Danger will reach the High Category
as a result of the wind and humidity combination. Additionally,
these strong winds may create blowing dust today, causing
visibility reductions at times.

possible.

following areas, in northeast Florida, Baker. In northern Florida,
Eastern Hamilton, Gilchrist, Northern Columbia, Southeastern
Columbia, Southwestern Columbia, Suwannee, Union and Western
Hamilton.

Cyclone Isaias passing northwest of the area will bring rounds of
moderate to heavy showers and thunderstorms across areas of
Southeast Georgia and the Suwannee Valley of Northeast Florida
today. Additional rainfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches are likely
with locally higher amounts possible.
